audiences.label: For citizens
audiences.level: General public — no science background needed
audiences.title: Will heavy rain flood more homes in Logroño, and do green spaces help?
audiences.lead: This study looked at every residential building in Logroño and asked how many residents are at risk when a short, heavy downpour floods the streets — today, with heavier future rain, and with more green space in the city.

sections.p: The study used computer flood maps of Logroño made by the REACHOUT project for 15-minute downpours, from storms expected every 2 years to storms expected once in 200 years. For each residential building it combined three things: how deep the water gets nearby, how many people live there, and how socially vulnerable they are. It compared today's rain with heavier future rain, the green measures planned in REACHOUT's scenario, and an extreme case where all open space becomes green.

sections.h: Heavier rain puts more people at risk
sections.p: With heavier future rain, more residents live in buildings at risk in every case examined: a few percent more in the middle scenario, and up to about one in ten more in the high one. How much more depends strongly on how much heavier the rain becomes, which is itself uncertain. Put simply, the flooding we expect today from a once-in-100-years storm could come roughly twice as often, or more in the high scenario. Data from the European Destination Earth project support the middle scenario's order of magnitude.

sections.h: The planned green measures help only a little
sections.p: The planned measures, as REACHOUT modelled them, reduce the number of residents at risk by a few percent at most, only for frequent storms, and not at all for the biggest storms (once in 100 or 200 years). In this model, they do not offset the effect of heavier rain.

sections.h: More green space helps — but not the people who need it most
sections.p: Turning all open space green takes roughly one in ten to one in five of the residents at risk out of risk. But these are mainly less socially vulnerable residents: in every comparison made, the residents who leave risk are less socially vulnerable than those who stay at risk, and the most vulnerable fifth of residents benefits least.

sections.h: What it means, and what it cannot say
sections.p: The study recommends placing green measures where vulnerable residents are at risk, not simply where there is open space, and checking the planned measures again with a model that includes sewers and storage, using their real layout. These are scenarios from one flood model, not predictions, and the uncertainties are large: the model has no sewers, the future rain is a scenario, vulnerability is estimated from census areas, and the measures may work differently when built. The direction of each finding is more reliable than its exact size.

audiences.closing: Heavier rain is expected, though by how much is uncertain; where green measures are placed decides who they protect.

audiences.label: For schools
audiences.title: Who is protected when a city goes green?
audiences.lead: Climate change makes heavy rain heavier. Cities can add green spaces, which let rain soak into the ground. This study asks a fair question: who does that protect?

sections.p: Logroño is a city in northern Spain. When a lot of rain falls in a short time, streets and underpasses can flood. This is called pluvial flooding: flooding caused directly by rain, not by a river. The study asks three things. Does heavier future rain put more people at risk? Do the planned green measures help? And when the city goes green, who is protected?

Scientists used flood maps made by a computer model. For every home building, they combined three things: how deep the water gets nearby, how many people live there, and how vulnerable they are — for example, young children or older people living alone. A '100-year storm' means a storm so strong that, on average, it comes once in 100 years. They tested storms from every 2 years to every 200 years.

Heavier future rain puts more people at risk in every case tested. The planned green measures cut the number of people at risk only a little, and not at all for the biggest storms. Turning all open space green helps more: roughly one in ten to one in five of the people at risk become safe. But most of them are the less vulnerable people. The most vulnerable fifth of residents benefits least.

sections.h: The lesson: how science checks itself
sections.p: Before using the method, it was checked. First, the method was rebuilt independently with open tools: every building got the same risk class as in the original study. Second, the flood maps were compared with places that really flooded in Logroño: they matched well, but this only partly confirmed the whole method, because real flood reports do not say who was affected. Finally, every result here comes from one computer model, with large uncertainties: for example, the model has no sewers, and nobody knows exactly how much heavier future rain will be. So scientists trust the direction of a result (more risk, small help, unequal help) more than its exact number, and they say so.

audiences.closing: Being fair is part of the science: a good plan asks not only how much it helps, but whom.
